tasks.hint:
Lists use zero-based indexing — the first item is at index `0`, second at `1`, third at `2`.
Access an item: `fruits[1]` gives `'banana'`
Common mistake: `fruits[2]` for the 'second' item — that's the third!
tasks.walkthrough:
Positions start at 0, so apple is at 0 and banana is at 1.
`fruits[1]` picks out banana.

tasks.description: Create `nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]`. Print the last element without using its index number.
tasks.hint:
Python supports negative indexing — `-1` always means the last item, regardless of list length.
`nums[-1]` is `6`, `nums[-2]` is `2`, etc.
This is useful when you don't know the length of the list.
tasks.walkthrough:
A negative position counts from the end, and -1 always means the last item.
That works whatever the length, so you don't need to know there are 8 items.

tasks.description: Create `fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']`. Add 'orange' to the end and print the updated list.
tasks.hint:
`.append(item)` adds an item to the END of a list — it modifies the list in place.
`fruits.append('orange')` then `print(fruits)` — the list now has 4 items.
Don't assign the result: `fruits = fruits.append(...)` is wrong — append returns None.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.append()` adds one item to the end of the existing list.
It changes the list directly, so you call it on its own line and then print the list afterwards.

tasks.description: Create `nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]`. Print the list sorted from smallest to largest.
tasks.hint:
`sorted(nums)` returns a NEW sorted list without modifying the original.
`nums.sort()` sorts in place and returns None — don't use it inside print().
Use `print(sorted(nums))` to print the sorted result.
tasks.walkthrough:
`sorted()` returns a brand new list in ascending order, leaving `nums` untouched.
Because it returns the list, it can go straight inside `print`.

tasks.description: Create `colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue', 'yellow']`. Print how many items are in the list.
tasks.hint:
`len(collection)` returns the number of items in a list (or string, dict, etc.).
`print(len(colors))` → `4`
This works on any sequence — very commonly used.
tasks.walkthrough: `len()` counts the items. It's a function you call with the list inside the brackets, not a method with a dot.

tasks.description: Create `nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`. Print True if 30 is in the list, False if not.
tasks.hint:
The `in` keyword checks membership and returns `True` or `False`.
`print(30 in nums)` → `True`
`print(99 in nums)` → `False` — the value doesn't need to be a variable.
tasks.walkthrough:
The `in` keyword asks whether a value appears anywhere in the list.
It produces `True` or `False`, and printing that gives the answer directly.

tasks.description: Create `letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']`. Print just the first three items using slicing.
tasks.hint:
List slicing syntax: `list[start:stop]` — stop is NOT included in the result.
`letters[0:3]` gives `['a', 'b', 'c']` — or the shortcut `letters[:3]` (start defaults to 0).
Slicing always creates a NEW list, it doesn't change the original.
tasks.walkthrough:
A slice with no start begins at position 0. The stop of 3 means positions 0, 1 and 2 are included.
`letters[0:3]` is exactly the same thing written out in full.

lesson.intro:
A list holds several values in order under one name. Shopping items, scores,
names, anything. Once you have a list you can look things up by position,
add to it, sort it, and loop over it. Lists are probably the most-used thing
in all of Python.

sections.heading: Making a list and picking items out
sections.body:
Square brackets with commas between the items. To get one item, put its
position in square brackets after the name. Positions start at 0, not 1,
so the first item is `[0]` and the second is `[1]`.

sections.heading: Counting from the end
sections.body:
Negative positions count backwards. `[-1]` is always the last item,
`[-2]` the one before it. That's handy when you don't know how long the
list is.

sections.heading: Adding, counting, checking
sections.body:
`.append(x)` adds an item to the end. `len(list)` tells you how many items
there are. `x in list` gives `True` or `False`.

`.append()` changes the list in place and returns nothing. Don't write
`fruits = fruits.append('orange')`; that replaces your list with `None`.
sections.code:
fruits = ['apple', 'banana']
fruits.append('cherry')
print(fruits)
print(len(fruits))
print('banana' in fruits)

sections.heading: Sorting
Slicing: a piece of a list
sections.body:
`list[start:stop]` gives the items from `start` up to but not including `stop`.
Leave out `start` to begin at 0, leave out `stop` to go to the end.
Slicing always makes a new list.

watch_out: The second item is `[1]`, not `[2]`. Zero-based counting is the number one source of list mistakes.
Asking for a position that doesn't exist, like `[5]` on a three-item list, gives an IndexError.
`fruits = fruits.append('x')` throws your list away. Just call `fruits.append('x')` on its own line.
